name: Omori's Law
statement: After a mainshock, aftershock frequency decays hyperbolically with time following n(t) = k/(c + t).
meaning: The law describes how the rate of aftershocks drops off rapidly but persistently after a large earthquake rather than stopping abruptly. Immediately after the mainshock aftershocks are frequent, and their rate falls following a power-law-like decay curve as time passes, with k and c being empirical constants fitted to each sequence.
mechanism: The decay reflects the relaxation of stress in the crust surrounding the ruptured fault as smaller subsidiary ruptures release residual stress. In 1961 Tokuji Utsu generalised the formula to n(t) = k/(c+t)^p, adding an exponent p (typically 0.7–1.5) that governs how steeply the decay rate falls, letting the model fit a wider range of sequences.

examples.text: Omori derived his 1894 formula largely from aftershock data following the 1891 Mino–Owari earthquake (magnitude about 8.0), Japan’s largest known inland earthquake.
Utsu’s 1961 modified formula is now the version most commonly fitted to real aftershock sequences, since it captures decay over a broader range of p-values.
For p about 1, the law implies that if the aftershock rate on day one is a given value, the rate on day two is roughly half, and by day ten roughly a tenth of the first-day rate.

whyItMatters: Omori’s law underpins operational aftershock forecasting used by seismological agencies to estimate the probability and rate of subsequent shaking after a mainshock, informing public warnings and emergency response.
limits: The simple form does not capture all sequences well; the modified law with exponent p is needed in many cases, and even it can fail for complex multi-mainshock sequences. The law describes average statistical decay, not the timing or size of any individual aftershock.
misreadings: It is sometimes misread as guaranteeing aftershocks will stop by a specific date, when the hyperbolic decay technically continues indefinitely at ever-lower rates. It is also occasionally confused with the Gutenberg–Richter law, which concerns magnitude distribution rather than decay over time.
origin: Formulated by Japanese seismologist Fusakichi Omori in an 1894 memoir; later modified by Tokuji Utsu in 1961.
